AN OLD NEGRO LYNCHED.
Persons Guilty of a Crime Hang Him to Keep Him Quiet.
MERIDIAN MISS JULY 80 CHARLIE
Persons Guilty of a Crime Hang Him to Keep Him Quiet.

MERIDIAN, Miss., July 29.—Charlie Burwell, colored, about 65 years of age, has been lynched near here. It was thought that he was concerned in the Farmer outrage, which occurred within a stone's throw of where he was hung. On the night of the Fourth of July Lewis Farmer and his wife, who run a small store about two miles from here, were murderously assaulted and left for dead, after which the store was robbed.

Later developments seem to fasten the lynching on the real culprits since it is learned that this old negro Burrell was promised a reward of $250 to ferret out the guilty parties. This became known to those concerned in the Farmer outrage and they are thought to have made away with Burwell.

LATE NEWS NOTES.
The phaeton once owned by General Grant has been sold for $14.

The government is interesting itself in Waller's case and seeking information on it.

Disciplining the letter carriers is causing some complaint, but the government is determined to keep it up.

A crusade is on at Macon, Mo., and the Sunday law is to be strictly enforced.

The unfortunate negro colonists who went to Mexico are returning in a deplorable condition.

Charles F. Lafe resigned as railroad and warehouse commissioner of Illinois. Ex-Congressman Fithian will succeed him.

It is said that the Union Pacific is making another effort to regain control of the Oregon Railway and Navigation company.

John J. Hoagland, cashier of the Adams Express company at Newark, Ohio, has disappeared, leaving a shortage of $1,196.
Forty business men and clerks of Macon, Mo., have been summoned before the police court for violating the Sunday closing law.

Henry W. Hoffman, associate justice of the Fourth judicial circuit of Maryland and an ex-congressman, died at his home in Cumberland.

Charles Burwell, a negro, aged 65, was lynched near Meridian, Miss., by men implicated in a recent double murder. He was about to betray them.

J. Walter Blubdon, son of a wealthy contractor, Guy Brown and Charles Lynch, small boys, were killed by a train in a suburb of Washington, D. C.

Ollie Simmons, aged 18, was drowned while bathing in the Walnut river near Arkansas City, Kan. There were fifteen or twenty boys in the water at the time, but none saw him go down and none missed him.

Six Democratic members of the Toledo, Ohio, council were arrested for refusing to obey the mayor's call for a meeting of the city council.

The attorney general has called upon United States Marshal Nix of Oklahoma for an explanation of the escape of a prisoner on the 'Frisco road some weeks ago, who was being taken to the penitentiary by William Nix, a brother of the marshal.

Governor Culberson's edict, adverse to pugilistic encounters in the state of Texas, does not seem to have had much effect on the sports, who take a deep interest in pugilism. They all believe implicitly in Dan Stuart's ability to bring off the big fight at Dallas.

The Chickamauga Park association has received notice of the contemplated attendance of twenty governors of states with their staffs at the dedication, September 18, 19 and 20.

The Orange, Texas, Athletic club has offered $40,000 for the Corbett-Fitzsimmons fight, and guarantees to pull it off without interference, on an island, the title of which is in dispute between Texas and Louisiana.

John Houston, white, for forty-five years a leader of the Osage Indians in the Indian territory, died at Pawhuska. The whole tribe is in mourning.

Western Cottage Organ and Piano factory at Ottawa, Ill., burned; loss $75,000.

Superintendent of Schools Massey of Virginia has obtained a $4,600 judgment against Sam Small for a slanderous publication in the Norfolk Pilot.

Richard Croker, the Tammany boss, says English politics are just as corrupt as those of New York.

Joseph Nolte, Arthur Waller and Tillie Hein were drowned while fishing at Otterdam, Iowa.

A. J. Whitman, ex-millionaire-mayor of Duluth, was convicted of forgery in San Francisco.

Highwaymen at Springfield, Ohio, shot and beat Electric Motorman Bennis Lawrence and robbed his car.

William M. Fredericks, murderer of Bank Cashier W. A. Herrick, was hanged at San Quinten, Cal.

John Hicks' four children burned to death at Big Stone Gap, Va.

Edward Bullett has been declared the legal head of the Creek nation.

Between grasshoppers and drouth Ontario farmers are about discouraged.

Alma Busche, aged 19, committed suicide in Kansas City, Kan., while insane.

Miss Susan B. Anthony had an attack of heart disease Friday, but soon recovered.

Four escaped negroes drowned themselves near Fort George, Fla., rather than be retaken with blood-hounds.

Alberta Stuart, a 14-year-old Boston school girl, was assaulted and thrown into Charles river and drowned.

William Willis, the presidential colored coachman, is dead.

A vessel loaded with arms and ammunition left Philadelphia to reinforce the Cuban insurgents.
It is said that James Gordon Bennett of the New York Herald is to marry one of the richest women in Paris.
Mrs. Leland Stanford will sell off 600 head of thoroughbred horses to keep the Leland Stanford, Jr., university going.
Edward Beecher, brother of the famous Henry Ward Beecher, and a well known minister, is dead, aged 92

MISSISSIPPI MATTERS.
Remarkable Fruit Yield.
I. C. Roberts of Cresterville
In talking recently he said:

"In 1886 I went to where I now have my home and secured the place. The land was very old, and if there is such a state of land in Mississippi, it was worn out. At any rate it was what we would call cast out land. I went there to practice my profession, but soon decided to give a little attention to horticulture, thinking I might one day grow tired of medicine and want to secure recreation by giving my attention to something else.

"I knew absolutely nothing about the fruits best adapted to that section, but I went blindly at it, and set out twenty varieties of peaches, about twelve of apples and four or five of plums. All have done well and I have made considerable money out of them. I selected one acre of land which was very poor and put it in peaches. That was in 1890, and since that time, exclusive of the present year, it has netted me over $400, and this year I have already sold more than $225 worth of fruit from the acre. The trees are bearing finely now.

"In 1886 I put out twelve pear trees and in 1893 they began a profitable yield, giving me that year, net, $75. In 1894 those twelve trees gave me $96 net, and this year I have already found it necessary to take an immense number of pears from them to save the trees from breaking and being completely ruined. I expect to make considerably more than $100 this summer. In 1887 I pulled several switches from those trees, and,
to experiment, planted them. About
twenty-five per cent. of them lived, and
this year they are producing a small
yield of as fine pears as any I have ever
seen. There is another fact which I
mention in connected with my orchard,
and that is there has not a year passed
but my orchard land has not yielded me
a good crop of peas, sweet potatoes or
cotton. I plant between the trees and
the crops grow well."

The Democratic Convention—Dark Horses

Jackson, Aug. 2.—As the time
approaches for the meeting of the State
Democratic nominating convention intense
interest is manifested here by the
friends of the various and numerous
candidates for honors and emoluments.
The convention, from the present outlook, will be the largest ever assembled at this capital. Not less than 1,000 accredited delegates are expected, besides hosts of friends of the candidates, who will come to work and log-roll for their respective champions.

A rumor is current in political circles that there is a deal on foot to bring out a "dark horse" for lieutenant-governor, and it is supposed to have in some way connection with or to affect the race for United States senator. As far as can be ascertained from expressions of loyal party men, such a course of proceeding is very much deprecated.

As claimed by them, there are two tried and true candidates for the position who have made open and straightforward canvasses of the State, to-wit: Hon. J. H. Jones of Wilkinson and Dr. A. H. Bays of Webster. The former is a lawyer of great ability and has served repeatedly in both houses of the legislature, and in the constitutional convention of the State, wherein he reflected honor upon his State and acquired for himself marked distinction and honors, and who also has been for many years a leading spirit in the political arena, aiding in shaping the course and achieving the success of his party. The latter, Dr. Bays, is no less worthy and distinguished, and well deserves the commendation of his friends. Their friends claim that it would be an egregious wrong to these gentlemen, after their arduous and expensive canvass, for a man who has made no canvass and incurred no toils and anxieties to come in at the eleventh hour and pluck the fruit.

A Lynching at Meridian.

Charlie Burwell, an aged negro about 65 years old, was lynched near Meridian one night last week. It was at first supposed that he had been hanged for complicity in some of the hold-ups and attempted murders in that vicinity, which recently has stirred the people to fever heat.

It was thought that he was concerned in the Farmer outrage, which occurred within a stone's throw of where he was hanged. On the night of July 4th, Lewis Farmer and his wife, who run a small store about two miles from there, were murderously assaulted and left for dead, after which their store was robbed. The perpetrators escaped, and at present several suspects are now confined in jail. As already stated, it was thought that he was one of the parties to the crime.

Later developments seem to fasten the lynching on the real culprits, since it is learned that this old negro, Charles Burwell, was promised a reward of $250 to ferret out the guilty parties, and this becoming known to them they went to his house, dragged him to Sowashee bridge and strung him from a beam.

emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A3:
Divers Will Die
JUST AS SURE AS HE IS TAKEN BACK TO FULTON FOR TRIAL.
All Roads Leading Into That Town Guarded-The Saloons All Closed Determined Men Will Do The Work.
From Wednesday's Daily Ledger.
From a source absolutely reliable

From a source absolutely reliable the LEDGER this afternoon learns that the very minute the officers make their appearance in Fulton with the negro murderer, Emmet Divers, there will be trouble of the worst kind. Late newspaper reports sent out from Fulton say everything is quiet in that town and that the law will be allowed to take its course, but a reliable citizen of Mexico who has just returned from there says that determined and quiet men, men of age and discretion, have made up their minds to burn Divers in the cabin where he committed the damnable deed and that all the officers in Callaway county cannot prevent it.

Every saloon in Fulton is closed by order of the Mayor and will remain closed until after it is known whether or not Divers will be taken back here.

All roads leading into Fulton are guarded by squads of men and all trains passing through the town are watched and searched.

All business in Fulton is at a standstill and nearly all the men are armed, waiting and more than willing to mob the negro.

If Divers is taken in the day time he will be held until night, tied in the cabin and the torch applied. This has been agreed upon.

Two or three deputy sheriffs went to St. Louis by way of Mokane after the prisoner, but it is not known when or how they will arrive, hence the guards that are stationed on every avenue leading to Fulton.

A report was current on the streets of Fulton to-day that Divers and guards got off the fast Wabash east of this city last night and started to walk to Fulton. This report cannot be verified in Mexico.

There is a rumor that Judge Hockaday has asked for state troops and it is thought that the militia may take the negro back for trial and protect him.

Col. I. W. Boulware told the LEDGER's informant that he would not defend Divers even if ordered to do so by the court. And Col. Boulware said no other lawyer would dare do it.

It is true that the people of Fulton are quiet, but it is also true, our informant says, that they are determined, and that Divers is just as sure to be burned as he is taken back there, unless state troops are on hand to protect him.

This is the true state of things in the Divers matter as they now stand in Fulton and vicinity.

Some traveling men, who came up from St. Louis last night, reported that the negro rapist and murderer, Emmet Divers, was brought up from there last night and driven at once over to Fulton. The livery stable proprietors in this city and Sheriff Stephens, when seen to-day, knew nothing about the report at all. Two parties got off the far side of the train when it stopped here and at once disappeared. This, no doubt, originated the report.
emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A4:
FEED THEIR REVENGE.

Mob Lynches Emmet Divers the Fulton, Mo., Murderer.

Exhibit His Body from a Telegraph Pole as a Lesson.

TO BURN IT TONIGHT.

Mob Will Take Negro's Body to Cain's House.

Will Then Set Fire to the Whole Thing.
TO BURN IT TONIGHT.
St. Louis, Aug. 15.—Emmet Divers, the negro who outraged and killed Mrs. Cain, near Fulton, Mo., a couple of weeks ago, and was brought here for safe keeping, was taken from the sheriff at Fulton obout 1 o'clock this morning by a mob and hanged to a railroad bridge.

Divers was taken from here yesterday afternoon by Deputy Sheriff Buchanan of Calloway county and arrived at Fulton some time after midnight.

Sheriff Buchanan left the train with the prisoner some distance from Fulton, and was proceeding with him in a carriage, when he was intercepted by a mob of more than a hundred men, who forcibly took the negro and hanged him, as above stated.

The latest report from Fulton is that 1,000 or more men from all parts of the country gathered this forenoon at the bridge where Divers was hanged, cut his body down and marched with it to Fulton where it was suspended to a telegraph pole as a public spectacle and a warning to all evil doers.

This demonstration was made at the special request of J. W. Cain, the husband of the murdered and ravished woman. It is said the body of Divers will be taken to the little house where Cain and his wife lived, the whole premises saturated with coal oil and the remains of the negro and all the effects in the building destroyed by fire.

ABOUT OUR PEOPLE.
There were fifty-two colored people killed during the months of March, Apr., May, and June.

Some men have honor and wealth thrust upon them, others inherit it, while another class receive it through hard and unremitting toil; grit determination and perseverance. To this latter number may be classed Mr. H Smiley, of Chicago, who with his wife is making a brief visit to this city, the guest of Mr. Richard Jones. Mr. Smiley is now on his way to New York to obtain new novelties to introduce to his patrons. Mr. Smiley is the leading chief or caterer in Chicago.—Col. American.

The store of Corner Bros. in this city was robbed Aug. 3rd. About $100 was in a small box in the cash drawer. The thief opened the drawer,

took the money and passed out into the street. Several cusomers were in the store and the street was filled with people. Vergil Booth, a Negro aged fifteen, was arrested and admitted that he took the money and hid it under the floor of the store.—St. Joe Mirror.

There is much rejoicing among the male portion of Chicago's colored population. Visions of blue uniforms, trimmed with brass buttons and gold lace, grow brighter as the days pass. The more ambitious are busy studyidg the army drill regulation, and training their voices that they may have the proper pitch when called upon to assume the leadership and give words of command to their fellows.—Ex.

Emmet Divers the perpetrator of the inhuman crime at Fulton Mo. deserved and should have received the severest punishment known. but we see no cause why there should be any except ion that lynch law should be tolerated in this case. There was evidently no attempt made by the officers to protect this half witted demented prisoner. And they full well knew that when they were bringing him back to Fulton for his preliminary hearing, they were bringing him through a slaughter house to an open grave.
Earnest Greene a promising thirteen year old boy of Washington D. C. was shot and almost instantly killed, by E izabeth M. Flagler August 2nd. Earnest was passing the Fagler residence with several other companions and seeing some fruit on the ground within reach, childlike, reached his hand through the fence to get it. Miss Flagler who is a white girl, seeing the young Negro from her upstairs window, fired twice. One bullet taking effect. After the shooting Miss Flagler, with a friend, drove to the police headquarters and surrendered to Supt, Moore, to whom she delivered the weapon. At the inquest the jury rendered a verdict acquitting her.

John E. Bruce in Boston Transcript has called our attention to the following Negroes who have been honored by royalty. The Black Roscius—lra Aldridge the great tragedian, who was loaded down with medals, the ensigns of various royal orders, the gifts of kings and queens whom he had charmed and delighted, by his magnificent impersonations of the characters he assumed. In 1877 Edwad Wilmot Blyden a fullblooded Negro born in the West Indies, was appointed by the president of the Republic of Liberia, Minister Plenipotentiary of that government at the court of St. James, and was received with marked consideration by her gracious majesty, queen Victoria at Osborne, July 30. 1878. Dr. Blyden was soon after elected an honorary member of the aristocratic Atheneum Club of London. He is an author and linguist of world-wide reputation.
emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A16:
EMMETT DIVERS HANGED TO A BRIDGE. The Negro Murderer of Mrs. J. W. Cain Lynched Near Fulton, Mo.
Divers, the negro brute, who robbed murdered and then assaulted the young wife of J. W. Cain, near here, three weeks ago, was about 12:30 o'clock this morning taken from the officers and hanged to a bridge, eight miles east of this city, and not far from the scene of his terrible deed. The hanging occurred at the Caldwell bridge. Public indignation is very bitter, and excitement is at fever heat. The body was placarded, "Legal Execution." The streets of Fulton are crowded with an excited and angry populace, who openly denounce the action of the officers, and the end is not yet.

DISAPPOINTED MOB.

There was a mob of 400 or 500 men in and around Fulton all last night who expected to hang the negro when he reached town. They were very mad when they found they were headed off. A large party of the disappointed mob went out to bring the negro's body to town threatening to hang it in the court house yard and defy any one to move it. Others are threatening to burn Divers' body in the court house yard. Saloons have all been closed since Monday. The sounds that emanate from the infuriated crowds bodes ill to certain officers and ex-officials, who are openly accused of having, after running the negro all over the country to escape mobs, and after returning him to within a few miles of town, permitted him to be executed by a mob. The officers deny this accusation, and assert that they left the train with their prisoner ten miles from Fulton to avoid the lynchers.

STORY OF THE LYNCHING.

Divers was indicted here at the circuit court on Monday, as told in the Chronicle, and thereupon deputy sheriffs J. E. Buckner and J. H. Buchanan started for St. Louis, to bring the murderer to this city for a speedy trial, conviction and execution. The officers, with Divers, left St. Louis, at 4:30 Wednesday afternoon, and his departure from this point was promptly wired here. That was the signal for quiet action. In a very few minutes a body of over 50 resolute men had perfected their plans for the lynching of Divers. The original intention was to have taken him to the little frame house in which he murdered Mrs. Cain, and after securely binding his arms and legs to have applied the torch and allowed him to have perished in the flames. The mob met the officers and Divers near this city, and although the deputy sheriffs pleaded with the determined crowd to permit the law to take its course, and also made efforts to prevent the rescue of the prisoner, the lynchers would not listen to the appeals. Deputy Sheriff Buchanan, Ed Buckner and J. J. Jackson, of New Florence, the driver, were in a surrey with the negro, en route to Fulton when the party arrived near the bridge and were halted by the lynchers. Divers also begged to be spared, and shrieked for mercy, as ready and strong hands siezed him and dragged him from the officers. A rope was quickly tied around his neck and the mob then hurried him off to the convenient bridge where the other end of the rope was fastened to a protecting timber, and Divers was pushed off and the work of the lynchers was completed.

Divers cries for mercy filled the air while the mob was preparing his impromptu gallows, and his frantic shouts died away only when his body dangled at the end of the rope beneath the bridge. The mob then went under the bridge to make sure their victim was dead.

CHOKED WITH PAPER.

The mob tried to stop Divers

The mob tried to stop Divers' frantic cries by filling his mouth with paper, but the negro continued to fill the air with cries for mercy. "You — brute, you didn't heed Mrs. Cain's appeals, and we will not save you. You will hang for your crime as a warning to others." The Sheriff with the Coroner and a posse went to the scene of the lynching and later the body of the negro was brought to Fulton. Besides the lynching party there were

about 100 farmers and a few citizens from Fulton who witnessed the mob's work. The lynching had been anticipated.

THE MOB'S RENDEZVOUS.

The mob chiefly came from Caldwell at which place Sheriff Laws and Deputy Sheriff Dundon were killed and a horse thief hanged two years ago. It was expected that Divers would be burned at the stake, as this was the plan agreed upon.

DIVERS' CRIME.

Emmett Divers called at the home of Mrs. J. W. Cain, four miles from Fulton, about 8 o'clock in the morning three weeks ago, and found the young bride alone. His motive was robbery, and when he attempted to take a ring from her finger she fought fiercely. She was finally overcome and the brute tied her hands and then secured the ring. The fiend in his frenzy after robbing the helpless woman, then drew a knife from his pocket and gashed her throat from ear to ear. As the woman lay weltering in her blood the wretch criminally assaulted her and then fled.

Her husband returning to the house several hours later, was almost paralyzed by the horrible sight of his young wife lying dead upon the floor of the kitchen. The alarm was given and Emmett Divers, a tough looking young negro living in the neighborhood, was captured. He denied his guilt, but a mob quickly organized to lynch him. The Sheriff spirited him away to Mexico and thence to New London, Hannibal and Bowling Green to protect him from armed mobs. Divers was finally taken to St. Louis' City Jail for safe keeping. While there he confessed his guilt.

HIS PARENTS FLEE

In the meantime his parents becoming alarmed over threats of lynching, and fearing the enraged citizens might seek their lives, last week hurriedly removed to Illinois. They passed through St. Louis, but refused to see their monstrous son in jail there.

GOV. STONE APPEALS.

Following Divers' crime, Governor Stone wrote appeals to Judge Hockaday counseling prompt efforts to prevent the disgracing of Calloway County by a lynching. The Judge indorsed the Governor's appeal, and for a time they had the effect of quieting the mob's plans. But when it became known that Divers was to be brought into the county yesterday the feeling for revenge overpowered the farmers and there was a general movement organized for speedy vengeance.

met Divers, was hanged at 1 o'clock Thursday morning at the bridge that crosses the stream at Calwood, in Callaway County, nine miles east of Fulton.

As stated in Wednesday's daily LEDGER the mob was on the lookout for him and every avenue leading into Fulton was closely guarded.

Deputies Buckner and Buchanan brought Divers out of St. Louis Wednesday afternoon on the Montgomery accommodation and left the train at New Florence. Late in the evening a conveyance was secured and officers and prisoner started for Fulton, knowing full well that Divers was being taken to his doom.

Near the little hamlet of Calwood the party was surrounded by the mob, the deputies made no resistance, a rope was brought into play, one end of which was tied around the negro's neck and the other fastened to the bridge, and he was forced to jump into eternity.

The mob was quiet but determined and the deputies knew it would be useless to attempt to defend their prisoner.

Arrangements had been made to burn Divers in the cabin where he committed the bloody deed, but the enraged mob thought as the time was opportune he had better be disposed of then and there.

Emmet Divers confessed that he outraged Mrs. J. W. Cain near Fulton, at 10 o'clock Tuesday morning, July 23, and then cut her throat eight times.

No more flendish crime of the kind ever occurred in Missouri. The victim of the negro's lust was a fine looking young woman, only 18 years of age. She was married to J. W. Cain, a prosperous young farmer living five miles from Fulton, last May. The negro entered the house when the young woman was alone, felled her to the floor with his fist, tied her right hand and neck with a rope, outraged her, murdered her, and walked coolly away. In the terrible struggle which she made for her honor the young woman's right thumb was severed at the second joint by the large knife which the negro carried in his hand. After he emerged from the house he wiped the blood from the weapon with his handkerchief and returned both to his pocket. His shirt was covered with blood and one of the buckles was torn from his suspenders. It was found beneath the body of the murdered woman.

In his confession Divers said: "I left home about 9 o'clock in the morning to look for work. I reached the Cain house about an hour later. The door was open and I walked in. The woman was sitting by the bed cutting out quilt pieces. I asked her if there was anybody there but her. She said no. I asked her to give me the ring she had on her finger. She said she didn't want me to have it. I then started to take it away from her and got it off her finger. It dropped to the floor. I then kocked her down with my fist. She started to get up. I saw a rope lying on a chair and tied her right hand to keep her from fighting me. I then put the rope around her neck and drew it as tight as I could. She kept trying to fight me and I cut her throat."

Afterward Divers admitted that he outraged Mrs. Cain before he killed her.

Just after the deed was committed Sheriff Windsor, fearing a mob and desiring to uphold the dignity of the law, spirited the negro away from Fulton. He was brought to Mexico, and still fearing a mob, he was taken to Bowling Green. From there he was taken to New London and later to the Four Courts prison in St. Louis, where he remained until removed by Deputies Buckner and Buchanan Wednesday evening.

HOW THE JOB WAS DONE.

The Auxvasse Review of Thursday, in its account of the lynching of Divers, says:

J. Ed. Buckner and John Buchanan were sworn in as special deputies to bring the negro from St. Louis.

Mr. Buckner left Auxvasse Tuesday morning, ostensibly for Keytsville, and Mr. Buchanan left Mokane the same day. These gentlemen met in St. Louis and on Wednesday afternoon at 4 o'clock they left St. Louis with their prisoner. They came by way of the Wabash on the Montgomery accommodation and stopped at New Florence, in Montgomery County. From New Florence they started with the prisoner overland to Fulton, a distance of 35 miles. The deputies knew the stations from Montgomery City up were closely guarded and thought to avoid the mob by leaving the train at New Florence.

They proceeded on their way unmolested until they came to Dr. J. N. Tate's place, two miles and a half west of Calwood, where they were halted by a band of fifty or more masked men.

Mr. Buckner said the negro was asleep when the halt was made and did not appear to be much disturbed when he knew what was up. The negro was the coolest man in the crowd.

The masked men commanded the
emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A18:
The command was obeyed on short notice and with about eight men in front and eight in the rear and four men on either side of the negro and deputies the procession proceeded to the Calwood bridge over the Auxvasse.

Messrs. Buchanan and Buckner protested with the masked men and begged them to take their prisoner on to Fulton and let the law take its course. A spokesman answered: "It is useless to try to persuade us from this thing. We have wives and daughters to defend. We mean business and we will have the scoundrel. Resistance is useless and we don't want to hurt anybody but the negro rapist and the negro we will have." And with that they took him.

When they had reached about the center of the bridge a halt was called and the negro was dragged out. About fifteen feet of rope was produced, one end tied around the negro's neck, the other to a brace on the bridge. Somebody said: "Jump, you black brute!" The bridge quivered and all was silent.

It was about 1 o'clock this morning when the negro was dragged from between the deputies and ten minutes later his worthless body was dangling between heaven and earth.

The deputies, Messrs. Buchanan and Buckner, arrived at Fulton and notified Sheriff Windsor and Coroner Davis about 3 o'clock this morning.

On leaving the St. Louis jail Wednesday afternoon Divers said: "Goodby, everybody. You will never see me alive agin,' for sure, when I get to Fulton I will be strung up. I killed the woman, but didn't intend to. It's a lie that I ravished her, but it's no use talking, for when they get me up there at Fulton I will be a dead nigger. They wanted to string me up at once, but the Sherlin was to slick for them and got me to St. Louis. If I must die, I'd rather it was in jail right here, for they will make me die hard."

MR. CAIN SATISFIED.

The Fulton Telegraph says: The Telegraph has just seen Mr. John W. Cain, husband of the murdered woman. He seems to be entirely satisfied, and says that he would only like to have had a short talk with Divers before he was lynched. He asks that peace and order be restored and that our citizens now resume their peaceful vocations.

WILD SCENES IN FULTON.

FULTON, Mo., August 16.—The town is in a measure quiet to-day to what it was yesterday, when everybody was wild with excitement over the lynching of Divers. The farmers have all gone to their homes and comparative quiet reigns this morning.

The disappointed portion of the mob affirms that but nine men composed the lynching party, and that they were instructed by county officers to do the work.

Some time after the lynching party had successfully finished their work, the mob, which had for days and nights guarded every possible entrance to the town, became aware of the proceedings at the bridge and the five or six hundred men who composed the mob started with horses at full speed for the scene. On arriving at the bridge and learning that they were two hours behind time, and learning also that only a very few men had composed the lynching party, they became infuriated and their curses of rage and disappointment were heard on every hand. Rumors of their having been betrayed by the county officers, who had by previous arrangements instructed the few who did the hanging where Divers might be taken, were soon afloat and the officers loudly condemned.

In full view of the court room where the Circuit Court is now sitting, and within 25 yards of the office of every county official and the rostrum of the Circuit Judge, on one of the main thoroughfares of the town, the mortifying body, horrible in the extreme, swung all of yesterday afternoon, an evidence of the vengeance of an outraged man and sympathizing fellow-citizens.

At 2:15 p. m. a howling mob of over 500 horsemen rode into town with the body of the negro in a farm wagon. They followed the principal street to the Court House Square, where the cavalcade stopped. The covering was thrown off the wagon and fully a thousand people took turns in viewing the distorted features of the corpse.

The march was then again taken up to the Fair Grounds in the southern portion of the city. Here, at the request of the murdered woman's husband, the body was taken from the wagon and swung to a telegraph pole.

Yesterday the Coroner impaneled a jury and visited the scene of the lynching. After examining the body a verdict, "death at the hands of persons unknown," was rendered. The body was brought to Fulton at noon Thursday by a mob of 200 men. They then formed a procession and marched, with the corpse, around the Court House, shouting "Let the law take its course." From there the mob marched to the old Fair Grounds, west of town, where the body was suspended from the limb of a tree and became a target for hundreds of bullets.

Half an hour later it was brought back to town, another rope secured, and the end, after being thrown over the crosspiece of a telephone pole in front of the Court House, was handed
emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A22:
Lynch Law in Callaway.
After the sheriff, of Callaway county, had succeeded in spiriting the negro rapist and murderer of Mrs. Cain to the St. Louis jail, it was hoped that the law would be permitted to take its course and that the brute would soon have meted out to him the just penalty of his crime by legal authority. The grand jury had indicted Divers, the circuit court was in session ready to try him and the deputy sheriff had gone to St. Louis to bring him to Fulton. Knowing that a mob had intended to wreak their vengeance upon the flend, the deputy put his wits to work to land the negro in the Fulton jail and thwart the purposes of the mob. In this, however, he was doomed to disappointment. He left St. Louis on Wednesday night of last week, in company with the negro and a Post-Dispatch reporter, came on the train as far as New Florence where they took a carriage for Fulton. They got along very nicely till some 10 miles east of Fulton, when they were halted by a dozen or more determined men, who made known their business and directed the sheriff to drive on, while they accompanied the carriage, guarding it closely. When they reached Auxvasse creek the ordered another halt and another body of men joined them. The sheriff made an earnest plea for the life of the negro, urged them to let the law take its course, all to no purpose. The men dragged the dastardly creature, nearly paralyzed with fright, from the carriage, put a rope around his neck, fastened the other end to the bridge and threw him off. He had a fall of about 10 feet which must have broken his neck.

The negro acknowledged to killing the woman, but denied committing the rape.

This was all done in the darkness of night, unknown to a large number of men who had assembled in Fulton awaiting the coming of the murderer. The body of the negro was brought into town after daylight and hung up to a lamp post, where it remained during most of the day.

We regret very much that the good people, of Callaway, county should have felt called upon to avenge such a diabolical deed outside the pale of the law, but if there is a crime for the punishment of which the people are justified in taking the law into their own hands it is the one for which this nend was put to death.

SATURDAY, AUG. 31, 1895.
LYNCH LAW

announcement recently, that 250 Negroes have been killed since January 1, '95. Where will this outrage end. This outlawry should be stopped if it takes the whole U. S. army to do it. There have been more Afro-Americans killed in the United States since 1865 than there were during the recent rebellion. B. K. Bruce, editor of the Leavenworth Herald, a leading Afro-American journal published at Leavenworth, Kan., in a recent issue had the following to say: The agitators may agitate, but as long as men assault women and children, lynching is sure to go on. The remedy lies in making a change for the better in the men who commit crimes. Stop the crimes and lynching will be no more."

The above is a full confession that these murderors and lawless elements of Anglo-Saxons are right in the whole sale butchery of our people. Our friend Bruce is not willing to grant to the colored people that right which is granted to the lowest white criminal in the land, a fair and impartial trial by twelve honest jurors, under the sanctity of their oath, who are instructed to give a fair and impartial verdict. If found guilty under the law and evidence, they should be given the extreme penalty of the law, and if not found guilty, acquitted. Herein rests our respect for the law.

We call Bro. Bruce's attention to an article clipped from an esteemed contemporary, the evening State Journal, August 17, written by W. L. Eagleson an Afro-American journalist of this state, which will furnish some very instructive reading matter for such men as he, as well as the public. The following is the communication:

To the Editor of the State Journal:

"A couple of Topeka young men masqueraded as colored men last night and fooled their own mothers."

The above clipping taken from the news and notes column of the Topeka Journal of August 16, reveals an alarming condition of things to colored men, for if these two masquerading young white gentlemen can so effectually disguise themselves as Negroes, so that their own mothers do not recognize them, it becomes serious, for we are confident, as it is designated by the press, that many "burly niggers" have been made the victims of this "joke" in the south.

W. L. EAGLESON.

What do you think of this, my Afro American friend? Honor bright, don't you think, friend Bruce, that the same thing is played on the colored people all over this country? Then if Anglo Saxons can disguise themselves as Afro-Americans so that their own mothers won't know them, in God's name, how do you expect innocent girls to distinguish the difference?

For your interest, Mr. Bruce, we'll give you a little more reading matter taken from the Capital of August 20:

"Benjamin Dunn, who for several years has the financial secretary of the Walnut Grove M. E. church, and who is a man 47 years old, was arrested by Policeman Long Sunday night. Dunn is charged with attempting to assault several little girls who were the children of other members of the church. His friends claim that he is demented."

We learn from reliable sources that Mr. Dunn has been released and allowed to go scot free, unharmed and unmolested. If this had been an Afro-American he would have been hung as high as Haman and his body riddled with bullets. To prove what we say, read this press dispatch note of the 16th "Emmet Divers, the perpetrator of the inhuman crime at Fulton, Mo., deserved and should have received the severest punishment known, but we see no cause why there should be any exception that lynch law should be tolerated in this case. There was evidently no attempt made by the officers to protect this half witted demented prisoner. And they knew full well that when they were bringing him back to Fulton for preliminary hearing, they were bringing him through a slaughter house to an open grave."

It is our opinion that Editor Bruce is seeking notoriety among our white enemies at the expense of his people. But if he puts his ears to the ground and listen to public sentiment among the better element of both white and colored of his city, he will immediately cease his warfare upon his poor, down-trodden brothers. We do not mean to wink at crimes, but we ask for that element which commit crimes to be tried before a court of justice and be sentenced like other criminals. The Herald evidently does not believe in law and order. To keep this lawless element from hanging you, he gives the following solution—Get wealth, culture and refinement. The above is good advice as far as it goes, but Mr. Bruce must have very poor memory or does not keep himself posted up on this all important question. Does he not know that educated and refined Afro-Americans are being outraged, whipped and murdered in the southland every day? Only a short while ago, some of the most refined and educated ministers of the gospel boarded a train at Birmingham, Ala.,

en route to Detroit, Mich. They were ordered in a second-class coach by the brakeman. They refused to comply with the brakeman's request, and a telegram was sent ahead to D.catur, Ala, and a mob boarded the train at that station, and the ministers were taken off the train and whipped until their backs were bleeding and their arms had to be carried in slings. My dear Editor Bruce, what do you think a mob cares for your refinement?

Our advice to you is to find a better solution for mob violence. Our solution is that any community that tolerates lynch law or lawlessness, when any citizen is struck down or lynched black or white, that community should be made to pay an indemnity to the widow or orphans of those who are murdered. We believe when this is done that this horrible butchery in this land will cease, and lynchers will be put behind the bars or hanged dead by the neck.

In order to progress we should concentrate our forces along down the line and all will be well.

Let us stand by one another. The highest object of some of our colored people is to drag each other down.

Be true to your frienbs. No one cares if his enemy goes back on him. But if our friends go back on us it hurts us.

Our public schools begin Sept. 11 The parents should see that their chil dren are in readiness and their books secured, and that they are put in school and kept there, it will do them good.

The Afro.Americans of this country are crystalizing a wonderful sentiment in their favor by honest and industrious habits. Let the goo work go on, and the Negro hating Anglo-Saxon will be defeated, notwithstanding they hate the Afro-American worse than the devil hates an angel.

Quite a number of the people may think that life among hotel waiters is a life of happiness; but it is not the case, especially here in Topeka. The average wages paid to colored waiters is $15 per month. The bell boys and porters $8 and $12 per month. A waiters hours for duty in first class hotels, he is supposed to rush from 5:30 a. m. until 10:30 a. m. and from 12:30 p. m. until 3 p. m., and from 6 p. m. until 8 p. m. Bell boys and porters from 7 a. to 8 p. m. Their rnles are strick and their fines are heavy. If they are late they are fined 25 cents, and for breaking rules which are many, 25 cents. Waiting table is a trade. A green waiter can run away more guests from a hotel than a bad bill of fare. The table waiters of today as a rule, are high school graduates, and if they had a strong organization they would get better wages.
emmett-divers-fulton-1895-08-15.A27:
Terrible times are ahead! We were not consigned to hades this week.

We hate to see a Negro's head swelled. It is a sign that he hasn't got anything.

Life is too short for us to waste in replying to short-sighted individuals who pose as editors.

All the colored newspapers in this country are in line for the Atlanta Exposition. Hurrah!

Another campaign paper, the New Missouri, has jumped into political harness at Kansas City.

Has Paul Laurence Dunbar stopped editing the Indianapolis World? Did he become disgusted with "our race" so soon?

He who breaks away from the beaten track and points out the errors of the race is a target for those who are in search of popular approval.

This paper has always advised our people how to become good, respectable citizens. It is with those who do right and against those who do wrong.

The colored people must learn to fight, to chastise those who do wrong, and to praise, upbuild and elevate those who do right. This is the true line to advancement.

The race needs more men and less fool preachers. Conscienceless and unscrupulous preachers are continually fleecing the people and taking the bread out of the mouths of their little children. The rascally whelps should be kicked out of the pulpit.

Some people are so egotistic that they imagine the earth will cease to rotate when they die. They forget that the earth was making her daily rounds at their birth and they are too bigoted to see by daily events that no man is great enough to be missed.

The preachers who run the Tribune of New Orleans would better put their thought in their sermons every Sunday. It would be food for reflection for church members and would possibly gain a few converts. There is not a particle of sense in it.

The Boston Herald and Globe complimented Marshall's band of Topeka during the Knights Templars' recent assembly in Boston. Jackson's colored band should have been in Boston also, so it could have surprised the natives of the effete East. We sincerely hope Jackson's band will attend the Atlanta Exposition.

The meanest cur on earth is a dog in human form. This dog is easily picked out in any community. In the first place, he does not take the race paper, then he is always talking about what is in it. He imagines that he is a critic, a newspaper man, as it were; a walking encyclopedia of knowledge, when, as a matter of fact, he is too ignorant to know that he is ignorant.

SENTIMENT AND LYNCHINGS.
Every man instinctively feels,

when he reads of some inhuman assault upon some woman or child, that the party or parties committing the assault should be punished. This is true of all, regardless of party, race or creed. The slow workings of justice have been the cause of Judge Lynch having so much to do. The sentiment of the following, taken from Republican and Democratic papers, is the same and shows that party politics cuts no figure when outrages have been committed, and that the only way to prevent lynchings is to stop the crimes:

ABOUT THAT LYNCHING.

We have received a communication asking the Globe-Democrat to raise a subscription for the prosecution of the men who lynched the Negro ravisher and murderer in Callaway county. Not a cent for prosecution, but millions for defense in a case of this kind.—Globe-Democrat.

No arm but that of a sentimental idiot would have been stretched forth to save the life of Emmett Divvers, the Negro who was swung to a railroad bridge in Callaway county recently for the rape and robbery of a white woman. In such cases the only rule of government should be a modification of the maxim of Davy Crockett so as to make it read: "Be sure you've got the right fellow, then go ahead with the hanging."—Brunswicker.

CREEK OUTLAWS CAPTURED. They Were Dividing the Spoils of a Raid When Surprised by Officers.
TULSA, I. T., Aug. 9.—The Creek Nation light horse police, three United States marshals, and a large number of citizens, captured Rufus Black and four other Creek negroes implicated in the Wilson assault forty miles south of Tulsa, upon Flat Rock Creek.

The outlaws had robbed a store at Orcutt, a small town near by, and were dividing the spoils when surprised. The officers started to Muscogee with them. A large number of citizens are in pursuit, with the intention of taking them away from the officers.

AGAINST THE MORA CLAIM.

Carlist and Socialist Deputies Will Issue a Manifesto.

MADRID, Aug. 9.—A meeting of Carlist and Socialist Deputies was held to-day at which it was resolved to oppose the payment of the Mora claim.

It was also decided to present a petition to the Queen Regent against the Government's decision to pay the claim, and, in the event of the failure of these measures, as a last resort, to issue a manifesto to the nation on the subject.

AMERICANS MOBBED AT TARSUS.

The Mission School Attacked and Some of the Students Maltreated.

LONDON, Aug. 9.—Advices received here from Asia Minor state that the American mission school at Tarsus has been attacked by a mob, and that some of the students were maltreated. The missionaries also were threatened with violence. No details of the affair have been received.

EXPELLED FROM VLADIVOSTOCK.

All the Jews in the Territory Ordered Out by the Czar.

LONDON, Aug. 9.—The Daily News will say tomorrow that the Governor of Vladivostock has been instructed to expel all Jews from the territory, under his authority, allowing them only time enough to wind up their business affairs and dispose of their immovable property. Several hundreds of Jews reside in Vladivostock.

rufus-black-okmulgee-1895-08-08.A5:
CRIMES OF A KIND.
Four Ravishers of Three Women Captured After a Fight.
CHECOTA, I. T., Aug. 9.—Rufus Buck, "Lucky" Bruner, Sam Simpson and Naomie July were arrested yesterday after a fight in the Concharty mountains, near Okmulgee. A few days ago these four, together with Louis Davies, ravished three white women, one of whom has died from her injuries. Davies escaped. More than a hundred men joined in the pursuit of these flends, but their capture was made by the Indian police, assisted by deputy United States marshals. It will require a strong guard to land the prisoners in the Fort Smith (Ark.) jail, as much excitement prevails and lynching is talked of.
rufus-black-okmulgee-1895-08-08.A9:
LYNCHING LOOKED FOR.
Three White Women Ravished, One of Whom Dies.
CHECOTAH, I. T., Aug. 9.—Rufus Buck, Lucky Bruner, Sam Simpson and Naomie Julie were arrested yesterday after a desperate battle in the Concharty mountains near Okmulgee. These four and Louis Davies ravished three white women a few days ago, one of whom has died from her injuries. Davies escaped, but will be caught. rufus-black-okmulgee-1895-08-08.A13:
DEATH TOO GOOD FOR THEM
Capture of the Fiends Incarnate of the Indian Territory—Two Attempts at Lynching Frustrated.
Wagonor, I. T., Aug. 11.—With the exception of one, the gang of Indians who committed a series of diabolical crimes since July 30 in the territory, were captured near Okomulgee last Thursday after a desperate fight and started for Fort Smith over the trail to avoid being lynched. News has reached here that a mob of citizens has gone across the line to intercept the Missouri Pacific train carrying the fiends and their captors for the purpose of dealing out summary justice. The gang, which began its heinous operations by murdering Deputy Marshal John Garrett at Okomulgee, and escaping to the hills of the Creek nation, was led by Rufus Buck, an Indian. His followers were Samuel Sampson, Merona July, Bud Lucky, alias Lucky Davis, Albert Stake and Levy Davis. The day after murdering Garrett the gang met a white man and his daughter in a wagon. Covering them with their guns the Indians took the girl from the wagon and each assaulted her within sight of her father.

Their next victims were Ben Callahan and a negro boy whom the gang met on the road. They murdered the boy and beat Callahan so that they believed him to be dead, relieving them of money, boots and saddles.

At the country store of West & Norburg, at Orkut, the murderers and robbers held up the owners and took away everything they could carry. Next in their path of crime they met two white women and a girl 14 years old. All were repeatedly assaulted by the fiends, who added another murder to their list. The girl's feet and hands were tied and the unfortunate creature was assaulted until life was extinct.

By this time the country in the vicinity of their crime had become aroused. Federal and Indian posses, including the Creek Light Horse Guards, in command of Capt. Edward Harry, and Deputies Jesse Jones, M. D. Irwin, Samuel Hayes and other determined officers, started at first to capture or kill the murderers of Garrett, that being the first crime heard of. Thursday afternoon the pursuers came up with the gang twelve miles from Okolmugee and divided, one half going to a place of ambush into which the other party drove the gang from the summit of a hill. A fight with rifles and revolvers followed, in which Captain Harry fell from his horse, a bullet grazing his head, and three horses were killed. Five of the gang were captured alive and the sixth, Lucky Davis, escaped.

In the possession of the murderers was 1000 rounds of ammunition and a great quantity of stolen property. They were taken to Okomulgee, where a mob of citizens bent on lynching them surrounded the officers, but the officers escaped with the prisoners to Muskogee.

Another mob, with ropes and rifles, awaited their arrival, but again the officers cheated the mob of its prey by getting sufficient warning to land the gang in jail. This was last night and the town was kept in an uproar all night by attempts to lynch the Indians and the efforts of the business men to prevent mob violence. The mob was finally quieted long enough to allow of a third escape of the posse and prisoners on a train for Fort Smith.
rufus-black-okmulgee-1895-08-08.A23:
A CHAPTER OF ATTROCITIES Unparalleled Record of Five Young Men. Indian Territory Fiends Lodged in Jail After a Ten Days' Career in Desperate Deeds—St. Louis Negro Turns His Revolver Loose on a Crowd of Steamboat Passengers—Durrant Trial.
Fort Smith, Ark., Aug. 13.—Rufus Buck, Samuel Samson, Meoa Judy, Lucky Davis and Albert Stake were lodged in the United States jail here to-day. All are young men who have in the past ten days made a criminal record for themselves which is almost without parallel in the Indian Territory. They murdered John Garrett, a negro deputy marshal of this county, about ten days ago. They met Mrs. Rosette Wilson two miles from Sapulpa, took her from the wagon and at the point of their revolvers outraged her, each assaulting her in turn. Two days later they went to the house of Mr. Hasson, between Snake creek and Duck creek, and all five assaulted Mrs. Hasson in the presence of her husband. They are charged with outraging two other women, robbing two stores and holding up three individuals. They robbed a stockman named Calahan and killed a negro boy who was with him.

The Buck gang sprung up suddenly about Okmulgee, flourished about ten days, and were taken in, but during that ten days they made a criminal record that fades the Dalton gang, the Starr gang or the Cook gang, considering the length of time they operated.

They started out on Sunday July 28, by killing a negro deputy marshal at Okmulgee. Rufus Buck himself is said to have done this job. After this Rufus Buck, Sam Samson, Meome July, Lucky Davis and Lewis Davis started out raiding throughout the country, terrofzing every section they visited. Four of them met Mrs. Wilson, who was moving from one farm to another with two wagons. Her fourteen-year-old son and a young man who was with her were made to drive on with one wagon, while they kept the woman and the other wagon. They made her get out and each one of them assaulted her, after which she was allowed to go her way.

Five of them a day or two later went to the house of Mr. Hasson, between Duck and Snake Creeks, and after forcing the lady to prepare dinner for them and partaking of it, all five of the scoundrels assaulted her, tieing her down with a rope. They then amused themselves by making Hasson and another man who was present fight each other and dance, shooting around their feet to make them move lively.

They met a man named Shafer on Berryhill Creek, eight miles from Okmulgee, robbed him of his horse, saddle and bridle, $50 in money and a gold watch. They then discussed the advisability of killing him, and took a vote on it. Three of them voted to let him go, and he was allowed to depart on foot.

They robbed a stock man named Callahan, even taking his boots, and then shot at him, one ball grazing his ear. At the same time they shot a negro boy who was with Callahan. He is said to have since died with his wound.

Lynching was freely talked of, and the citizens would certainly have been justified in putting an end to the whole gang, but being assured that the scoundrels would be turned over to Judge Parker's court, the officers were allowed to bring them in alive, and arrived here with them Sunday. They also brought in Albert Stake, who is charged with being implicated in the Garrett murder, but was not with them in the other depredations.

They will be indicted and tried during the present term of court. Buck is part Uche; Samson and July are Indians, while Lucky Davis is a negro.

THE PENDLETON GANG.

There is another little gang cropping out in the neighborhood of Red Fork, the leader of whom is said to be a young man, or boy rather, named Pendleton. One day last week as John Harks, the Sapulpa butcher, was making a trip between Red Fork and Sapulpa, he was held up by Pendleton and three other men and robbed of sixteen dollars, and all the sausage he had in the wagon. In exchange the robbers gave him a bottle of pine top whiskey.

The Crowell boys are said to be with this gang. No doubt they will soon be heard from again.

Day of Execution Fixed.
SMITH ARK SENTHAMBURG
FORT SMITH, ARK., September 26. — Rufus Buck, Louie Davis, Sam Sampson, Maomi July and Lucky Davis, all members of the Buck Gang, were brought into court yesterday morning and sentenced to hang Thursday, October 31. The crime for which they were sentenced was an assault upon Mrs. Hastings, near Okmulgee, Creek nation, on the 7th day of last August. Two other charges of the same nature were preferred against them but a trial upon these was unnecessary. All of the condemned men are Uchee Indians with the exception of Lucky Davis who is a negro. When asked by Judge Parker if they had anything to say why sentence should not be passed upon them, all with the exception of Lucky Davis replied that they had not. Davis remarked that he "wanted his case to go to the supreme court." It is not likely that an appeal to the supreme court will be taken as the evidence against them was so plain and convincing that the case was submitted to the jury without argument. Louie Davis and Lucky Davis are also convicted of murder.
